newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Philip Morris dividend play.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Philip Morris dividend play.

text.p: Volume in Philip Morris Cos Inc call spreads stood out in an otherwise relatively thin equity option market as a sharp selloff in underlying stocks scared most investors to the sideline, traders said.
Philip Morris calls dominated the American Stock Exchange most-actives list, apparently as professional institutions traded in huge sizes, they added.

"They buy and sell spreads, exercising the long calls today so that they'll receive the dividend and hoping that all their short options are not exercised tomorrow," said Michael Schwartz, a managing director of Oppenheimer and Co.
"The exercise results in a dividend capture with very little money almost risklessly," he said.
Philip Morris December 100 calls traded 56,069 contracts by mid-afternoon, while December 95 calls had turnover of 18,665, January 70 calls 15,175 and January 60 calls 14,175.
They were all deep in-the-money calls as the stock, which goes ex-dividend on Thursday, stood at 116, off 7/8.
Rod Jamieson, vice president of options strategy at EVEREN Securities, said there seemed to be little retail participation in the dividend play.

Elsewhere in the market, activity in Intel Corp options was also fairly busy as the stock shone as one of the few bright spots in today's battered overall market. "It seems like Intel's holding up all these semiconductor stocks that are barely down or unchanged," Jamieson said. Intel stock was up 3-1/2 to 132-5/8 in mid-afternoon trade after the company said its chip-making factories were at full production and that it expected robust sales growth. December 130 and 135 as well as January 130 calls each had turnover of around 5,000 contracts.

Implied volatilities were at the higher end of their recent ranges but were not outstandingly high as Intel has had relatively good two-way flows for a while, traders said. Volatility for December 130 calls stood at 39 percent and for January 130 puts slightly higher at 41 percent.
"Put it this way -- the stock is up four bucks, so you're not going to find a cheap option," Jamieson said.

He noted that out-of-the-money puts seemed to have slightly higher implied volatility levels, probably reflecting demand for protection against a pullback in the stock price amid the fragile market environment now. ((Shin Kishima 312-408-8750 E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com))
